MR. LAPRISE-REPORTED INCORRECT STATEMENT BY AGRICULTURE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all hon. members in view of the fact that on April 28 last the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) gave a false reply to a question I had directed to him. That question can be found on page 689 of Hansard and it read as follows:
Would the Minister inform the house whether he has replied to the letter sent to him by the Quebec minister of agriculture. Mr. Courcy, requesting assistance for farmers in Abitibi-Temis-camingue? If not, does he intend to do so in the near future?
The minister answered:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
Later on the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) asked the minister the following supplementary question:
The minister replied that he had assured farmers in northwestern Quebec that they would receive help. Could he tell us what is the nature of the assistance he intends to give them?
The Minister of Agriculture answered:
I said I was going to answer the letter.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have here a letter from the deputy minister of the federal Department of Agriculture which prompts me to ask some questions. That letter is addressed to Dr. Ernest Mercier, deputy minister of agriculture in the province of Quebec, and is dated from Ottawa, April 22, 1965, that is six days before the answer given to me by the minister on April 28. I quote the letter sent to Dr. Ernest Mercier: [Text]
Before my minister left Ottawa last week, he asked me to tell you that it had been decided that the Government considered it should not participate in payments to farmers for crop losses in Quebec 1964.
Your very truly,
S.	C. Barry,
Deputy Minister

The content of this letter shows clearly that a decision had been taken long before April 28, and that in spite of that fact the minister misled the house in deliberately giving a wrong answer.
Here is my question of privilege. Why is the government refusing to help farmers in the province of Quebec although a request has been made to that effect? Is the minister aware that Quebec is still part of Canada and that the government is not so penny pinching when it comes to granting similar assistance to other provinces or other countries?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DOMINICAN REPUBLIC-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he is in a position to give a report to the House regarding events which are taking place in the Dominican Republic. Is he in agreement with the President of the United States that communist conspirators are endeavouring to turn the Dominican Republic into another communist base? Has he given assurance to the Government of the United States of the support of Canada in any action they may take to prevent this area becoming a communist country?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DOMINICAN REPUBLIC-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has been in touch, through its embassy in Washington, with the United States Government with regard to the tragic developments in the Dominican Republic; it has been recognized that the United States Government has intervened in the Dominican Republic for the protection of its own citizens as well as 
DEBATES	May 3, 1965
those of other countries. It is recognized also, Mr. Speaker, that evidence has been stated to exist indicating intervention in the Dominican Republic with a view to bringing about a Castro type government in that island.
I am not able to assess the significance of that evidence at the present time. I do realize that, as President Johnson has already stated, the responsibility for the restoration of stability and security in that unhappy country, apart from the responsibility which attaches to its own people, is in the hands of the Organization of American States, and that organization has at present a committee of five in the Dominican Republic.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I could also give the House a word about the position of Canadians on the island. Officials of the Department of External Affairs have been in telephone communication with the officers of the Canadian Embassy in Santo Domingo Saturday, Sunday and this morning. The Embassy reported that a further 11 Canadians were evacuated over the week end and others were expected to leave today. All Canadians, wives and dependants, who wished to leave have left. Officials informed us this morning they are maintaining contact with several Canadian citizens who have elected to remain in Santo Domingo, in order to extend any further assistance and keep informed of their welfare. There are no reports of Canadian casualties.
Outside of Santo Domingo there are approximately 110 Canadian citizens. According to present reports none of these appear to be in danger. However, should the civil disturbances spread to the countryside, evacuation facilities will continue to be available for Canadians living outside the capital as well as those in Santo Domingo. The Embassy has been in touch by telephone with Falconbridge Nickel plant about 40 miles from Santo Domingo and reports the plant is operating without difficulties, although they may start today to evacuate some of their personnel.
The Embassy is also investigating reports that the main branch of the Royal Bank of Canada has been looted.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is accurate to equate the situation in Santo Domingo, tragic as it may be, with the situation in Cuba to which my right hon. friend referred, when the question was one of active intervention by the Soviet Union in Cuba. There is no situation of that kind in Santo Domingo so far as I know at the present time.
In so far as the intervention in the rebellion in Santo Domingo by elements that are attempting to bring about a communist takeover is concerned, we have not received sufficient evidence from the United States authorities-and we are in touch with them on this matter-to justify any conclusion on our part at this time. So far as the Organization of American States is concerned, we have been following the discussions of that body, of which we are not a member, and we view with interest and concern the step they have taken, which I have already reported to the House, in sending a committee to Santo Domingo with a view to bringing about a cessation of hostilities and the resumption of peace.

The fee we

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, April 30, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L.
May 3, 1965	COMMONS
Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it might be well at the beginning to review the amendment which was moved by the official critic of the Conservative Party, the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). The amendment reads:
This House regrets that the Government has failed to meet the most pressing economic problems of the country by refusing to abolish the sales tax on production machinery, which tax continues to penalize the manufacturing industry and business, thereby undermining Canada's competitive position in markets at home and abroad: and by not giving adequate relief from taxation for the lower income groups and increased assistance to old age pensioners in the face of the steadily rising cost of living.
I suppose by now the Minister has read with some interest the editorial comments in various newspapers and the headlines about the 10 per cent tax cut. The sunshine budget, the expansionary budget, has now been somewhat exploded. This has happened at a time when we had borrowed a slogan from the United States. I believe it was about a year ago this January that the President of the United States, in his address to Congress, mentioned that his Government was preparing war on poverty. If this was to be a budgetary war on poverty, may I suggest to the Minister at the outset that it has become a war on the poor.
This budget has given little if any relief to those in the lower income brackets. The Minister said it was a 10 per cent cut. Actually this is a misrepresentation, when you realize that this year the relief does not start until July 1. It becomes, therefore, a tax cut of 5 per cent. In this bracket in which we have, as the financial critic mentioned, two thirds of the population of Canada I will say on submarginal salaries, this tax cut becomes a reduction of about one cent per day. This is the reason I label this budget as not a war on poverty at all but a war on the poor.
I am going to deal with these points separately. The second thing is the failure of the Government to abolish the sales tax on production machinery used by manufacturers. This means an increase in the cost of production at a time when the Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, stated that manufacturers in Canada must be prepared to cut their costs so they can compete in world markets and so they can stay in business.
DEBATES	841
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams This is not only a tax on production machinery, but at the outset I would say it is a surtax, as the Minister knows, when the sales tax is imposed on the production itself. It amounts to double taxation. If Canadian industry is going to compete with United States industry or any other industry in the western world or the communist bloc, then I ask how can it compete when the Government itself imposes a sales tax on production machinery?
I believe the Minister, in his own heart, believes that the tax should be abolished. I believe he would like to abolish it. However, it is the last thing remaining from his original budget, from which he retreated so much, and if he were to retreat from this there would be nothing left of that budget. The manufactures have been told they must cut costs or they cannot compete. The Minister is placing a stumbling block in their path which prevents costs being cut because the sales tax creates a surtax. How can our industries compete with those of the United States and other nations?
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
During this session and the last session we heard a great hullabaloo about a contributory pension plan. The government has done nothing to relieve the position of senior citizens whose pensions, as with veterans and any other pensioners, are a frozen, set income; and when this is considered in the face of the ever escalating cost of living and the cheapened dollar, it means a great hardship. In other words the contributory pension plan and the budget ignored the needy and the aged.
In a nutshell what the Government did in this budget was to accomplish nothing except, to put it in round figures as someone else did the other day, the Cabinet Ministers increased their own salaries by $600, because that is what the tax cut means to them. They declared war on the poor and they increased their own salaries by $600. The Minister laughs, but that is why I say it is a war on the poor and not a war on poverty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You benefit too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; in reply to the Minister I benefit by $600, but I am not saying this is a philosophical argument as to the logic of what the Government has done through the budget. That is no explanation whatsoever.
On this indictment I ask all parties in the Opposition to give consideration to voting for the amendment on three grounds; (1) that
May 3, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams the Government failed to abolish the sales tax, which means added costs to the manufacturers; (2) that it declared war on the poor rather than war on poverty; and (3), it failed to consider the demands and the pressures on the pensioners of this country, particularly the senior citizens.
I may tell the Minister I have spent some time reading a rather famous speech he made when he was the financial critic of the Liberal party and sitting just about where I am today. If it was not his maiden speech it was his first financial speech in the House, and the date was October 22, 1962. In it he laid down 9 or 12 points containing his master plan.
What were the criticisms he offered on that occasion? One was in regard to the imbalance of trade between the United States and Canada and, if I interpret him correctly, on that occasion he said that if payments between the United States and Canada, and between other trading nations and Canada, continued in imbalance it would mean an increase in unemployment and create an economic situation that would be difficult to solve in terms of the conditions laid down by the Economic Council of Canada, which was a creature of the Conservative government and which has said we must have 1,700,000 new job opportunities created between now and 1970.
When I listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on Friday afternoon last, and to the Minister of Finance earlier, it almost appeared that they were the ones who invented prosperity. I only wish some of these Ministers would be honest and admit that our economic resurgence is really the result of economic prosperity in the United States and in the western world generally, reflected in Canada. Economic resurgences have occurred from time to time, and there are graphs which show the occurrence of recesses and deflation.
If the Minister of Finance had been fair, and if the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is unavoidably absent today having gone down to the United States, had been fair, they would admit that the gross national product in 1962, the last year the Conservatives were in office, increased by 8 per cent. We did not take all the credit for that at that time. We appreciated there was an upsurge in business in the western world generally.
Let us face up to the facts as economists rather than as politicians, and try to paint the


picture in its true colours. Let us look at the imbalance of payments for a few moments. In October, 1962 the Minister of Finance made a startling attack on the Conservative government. He said that an imbalance of payments between the United States and Canada would eventually mean unemployment. It is true that because of the upsurge in business there is less unemployment today, but what will happen to us when the United States gets into difficulties? What will happen to us when the western world is suffering economically? If the Minister was right then, he is wrong today.
What is our imbalance today with the United States? When I posed this question on Friday afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce said it was only $500 million. I say, let's do our homework. Before posing that question I called the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to see if I could get an honest answer, and I must say I got an evasive if not dishonest answer from the Minister. I found that at the end of the year our fiscal imbalance in trade with the United States was $1,379 million, something which can be checked by the press of the country and by the Ministers themselves.
Somebody says well, what is a billion dollars? I don't know. I don't suppose I will ever see that amount, but the fact remains that our imbalance was $1,379 million while the Minister said it was only $500 million. In 1962, when the Minister criticized the Conservative government, our imbalance of trade with the United States was less than $1 billion. It is now in worse shape by $500 million, yet the Minister was the man who had a master plan, a cure-all for Canada. How does he reconcile the position he took in October 1962 with his position today, when we have an imbalance of trade with the United States of $1,379 million?
In 1962 he read his speech, which was well prepared, and he left the impression that the Conservatives were responsible for that situation. But anybody who has read anything about economic history knows that in 1957 when the Conservatives took office the imbalance was more than $1 billion, and we improved that situation.
Let us take a look at the over-all picture and see whether this is a sunshine budget or not. Our trade with other nations gives a little better picture, because we have a favourable balance of payments situation with some nations as a result of our wheat deals and, for instance, our coal deal with Japan.
May 3, 1965	COMMONS
With all other nations we have an imbalance of trade totalling $652 million; thus our trade imbalance is in a worse position now than at any time the Conservatives were in office.
The Minister was the master mind who was going to cure all our economic ills, but all he can say today-and I must say I am somewhat jealous of him because he can say it-is that things are good. Things have been good since 1962. Things have been good in Europe since 1962, and things have been good in the United States since 1962. If Canada were to have a recess when all the western world was buoyant, then there would be something wrong.
I should now like to put on record what the Minister said on October 22, 1962, as recorded at page 817 of Hansard for that date. You know, Mr. Speaker, when these politicians come in they are great fellows to start with. They have a five year plan or a 12 point program, but they always forget it once it goes into a Hansard volume and is placed in the library. This is what the Minister said:
As the third point In the program, it is clear that we cannot go on paying more to foreigners each year for goods and services than we receive from them for the things we sell to them. To do this would lead only to another exchange crisis and it would mean the continuance of the present problem of finding jobs for people who are unemployed. The right policy for Canada in these circumstances is to increase production in this country, wherever this can be done without increasing costs.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Let us analyze what he said in October 1962, because this was the Gordon manifesto, this was the Gordon who was going to cure everything. He said we could not continue to buy more from foreign nations than we sell to them. But what has he done about it? He has done nothing. The imbalance of trade with the other nations of the world is higher than it was under the Conservative administration, and as high as it was in the time of the former administration in 1956 and 1957. But the point I am making is this. On top of it all, in his first budget he proposed and implemented a sales tax on production machinery. His last words in that paragraph are words to remember: "The right policy for Canada in these circumstances is to increase production in this country without increasing the cost." Well, he did the very thing he said should not be done, and he did it through taxation.
How has the economy been able to remain as buoyant as it is? I admit it is buoyant. No one will deny that the business of the nation

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams is good. It was good in 1962. But let us see what someone else had to say about the situation. The Minister of Finance is most fortunate that the Conservatives consummated wheat deals with the communists. I have heard him say so in the West when he goes there to throw out his chest and boast about this accomplishments. He does not remind them that it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce who advised them not to grow more wheat because there would be a surplus leading to reduced prices. If he had not had behind him the former Conservative Minister of Agriculture and the Conservative party to see that the wheat was produced and, above all, to consummate these contracts, he would be facing a serious exchange problem today. I will quote as my authority the former Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers. This is what he said on January 28, 1965: "Obviously, the devaluation of the Canadian dollar has contributed to the progress made in the last two years."
I might pause there for a moment. The Minister does not like to be told that. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, and in particular the Prime Minister, went across this country saying that the devaluation of the dollar would mean higher cost to consumers and restricted opportunities to the primary producers of this country. Now they say this was a good policy. Mr. Towers says the policy is a good one, but there is one aspect of it which must be watched carefully. Every time something is created there is a backlash. What is the backlash attached to the devaluation of the dollar? Maybe a year from now what I am saying will seem more important than it does now, because Graham Towers is a man who has had some experience and I believe I understand exactly what he means when he says:
it is well to remember, however, that devaluation produces certain painful results. It means amongst other things, that we pay more for our imports and tend to receive less for our exports-therefore, the terms of trade turn against us. Hopefully, lower prices for export products will stimulate demand for these goods, but it does make it more difficult to cure the trade deficit, as we must sell that many more units to earn the same income.
As far as a layman can judge, 1965 will be a good year. But what comes next? What is the point I am making? It is this. In order to derive full benefit from the devaluation of the dollar, which was Conservative policy, the Minister of Finance should have created a climate favourable for the expansion of
May 3, 1985

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams industrial and manufacturing concerns in this country, enabling them to reduce costs and prices. Instead he imposed a sales tax which had the direct effect of increasing costs. If there is to be a backlash consequent upon pegging the dollar, the Minister is responsible for that backlash inasmuch as he introduced measures which increased the cost of production. That is the situation.
In summary, on this point, let me say this. If we have a prosperous economy today it is due in the main to the influence of prosperous economies in the rest of the western world. Though the Conservatives, when in power, devalued the dollar, they did not impose a sales tax to increase the cost of production. We tried to create a climate favourable to export sales. Had there not been sales of wheat amounting to a billion dollars the Minister of Finance would have been in trouble. He has only been pulled out of trouble by the action taken by the previous Government.
I come now to my second point. As everyone who has spoken earlier from this side of the house has said, the reductions in taxation which the Minister announced mean nothing. The effect on those in the lower tax brackets is infinitesimal. The effect in the medium bracket is small, and even with regard to people in the higher tax brackets the effect on capital investment will be very slight. We have a progressive system of taxation in Canada similar to that which exists in other capitalistic nations; and here, I would say, we need reform.
I say this because on one hand we talk about foreign ownership of our industry, and on the other we take away so much money from those engaged in production in this country that nothing is left to invest in our nation. Professional and business men and corporations are well aware that the biggest partner today in any industry today is the Government. I am certain the Minister is aware of this, too.
I am talking about taxable income; I am not talking about income. The Minister himself is confused on this point, as can be seen from one of the schedules printed on page 444 of Hansard. He has confused taxable income with net income. I am one of those who believe it is not a sin to make a profit. I say this. The only way to increase the gross national product in this country is through investment, and the only kind of capital produced in this country which creates funds for investment of this kind is that which flows

from production, not from Government spending or Government enterprises upon which public money is spent.

speechtext: I must say to the hon. Member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) that I do not see any point of privilege.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason for his interjection was to try to get me off my stride, so that he could make a little press for
May S. 1965	COMMONS
himself. Because he is never capable of making a speech himself.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If he can hold on to one seat, he is lucky.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right; I must agree with that. Why has the Minister failed Canada? He and other Ministers have been going across the nation talking about putting the financial matters of Canada in shape. I have pointed out the imbalance of payments and what effect the income tax deductions have had. In fact, when the Minister brought down the first budget, which was a budget of retreat and of confusion, he had to withdraw everything in it which he proposed because he was so inept. The newspapers at the time, even his great friend the Globe and Mail, spanked him for that.
Now, what has happened since that time? This great lion-hearted critic of October 1962 has now been reduced to a mere lamb, and he has to bring in the most innocuous Budget today because he cannot stand any criticism. If he questions my word in this regard let me take for a few moments an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail on June 21, 1963. I shall quote only a small portion, and if I should violate the rules I can paraphrase it practically word for word. Talking about the budget it said:
If this is not enough to persuade Mr. Gordon of his duty to resign he should remember that the Liberals were elected to restore confidence in Canada abroad. They had considerable success in this direction until a week ago. Mr. Gordon by his ineptitude and-let us be frank-simple bad judgment has destroyed that confidence, as shown by an editorial in The New York Times quoted on this page yesterday. It does not matter if that newspaper is right or wrong in its judgment. The fact is that this is what our friends abroad are thinking, and thinking this way they cannot have confidence. Thus Mr. Gordon has prejudiced the record.
Then the final sentence:
Mr. Pearson may not want to accept Mr. Gordon's resignation, but Mr. Gordon should insist on delivering it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, why do I make this point? Although it may be said that I am hurting the Minister's feelings, the point is that when he was sitting on this side of the House in opposition he was the lion-hearted critic; but now, because of his failure, he has become a lamb and has produced this innocuous document which he calls expansionary measures for Canada.
Somebody mentioned the Minister of Agriculture's talks. No doubt the Liberal Agriculture Minister will deny that he made this
DEBATES	845
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams statement, but my hon. friend did say that the only policies which were any good for agriculture were those of the Conservatives, and he only ran as a Liberal because he thought the Liberals might win and he wanted to carry on those policies.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did he say that behind the barn?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, this was not said behind the barn; this was said outside the front door right beside the manure spreader.
I turn now to a third point. As the trading world expands the western world is trading more with Communist nations, and must do so. The Liberals criticized us at the time when we traded with the Communists in grain. I see the hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) is not in his seat today. He is one who is so critical of absenteeism, yet he was not able to collect enough chicks from his own members to propose any motion of his own to this House the other day.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ha, ha.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Someone says "ha, ha", but he is one who criticized wheat sales to Communist China. As we expand we in the Western world must deal not only with Communist nations but also compete with Western nations, such as the United States, Japan, France, Germany and others. We also have to be prepared now as never before to compete against the Communist bloc.
If I may come back to a point I made earlier, the Canadian system of progressive income tax which has developed in this country and other capitalistic countries over the years must be reviewed and reformed. We have only to look in this regard at such experts on the subject as Mr. W. O. Twaits, who made a comment about this in July of 1960 in an article entitled "Philosophy of Realism". The Minister of Finance was going to reform taxation, but now the Government says that while a Commission is studying the matter they cannot do anything about it. The fact is they are frightened to do something about it because they have no policies. They know that if they had cut taxes they might have had a greater deficit, which is the reason they did not cut taxes. But why not tell the Canadian people the truth?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, why? Let us see what Mr. Twaits said in his article of July 1960:
In editorial pages and current commentary, one is struck by an increasing preoccupation with the
846	COMMONS DEBATES	May 3. 1965
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams
philosophy and objectives of our western democratic system. There is an increasing awareness that our ability to compete with the Communist world is not just a matter of missiles and ideology, but also of our basic economic strengths.
Now let me come to another point. A philosophy of socialistic policies has grown up in Western Canada. Some people believe that it is a sin to make a profit. Even the people living within the Communist bloc today believe you must make a profit. You must have capital to produce investment and productivity. If you have investment with productivity you get an increase in the gross national product.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. Member but his time is up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure we would all be disappointed in not hearing more from the hon. Member. I certainly hope he will continue, but not for too long because some of the rest of us want to speak this afternoon.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I appreciate that from the Minister of Finance and I will be only a few moments. If it were not for the progressive system of income tax, labour unions would be less prone to ask for an increase in wages. Corporations would be less prone to increase their prices if they did not have 50 per cent taken off their profit level to reinvest, bringing about expansion in the country. I ask the Minister to take a look at this question, because we do need reform of the progressive system of income tax.
In summary, and leaving out some of the remarks I intended to make, I say that what Walter gives, Walter takes away. In fact, what Walter gives, Walter takes more away. That is what industry knows today and it is the socialistic philosophy of the Government. In fact, I believe that the Liberal Party is a New Democratic Party in a hurry. They have out-socialized the socialists of our time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know my hon. friends do not want to hear that, but nevertheless it is the fact. It is a fact which cannot be denied.
There are two other points I want to make, Mr. Speaker, one of which is this: When the Minister stood in his place the other day to

reply to a question I asked him about the table which compared Canadian and United States income taxes, he said that Canadians pay less income taxes than Americans. Let me remind the Minister that Mr. Lambert, the president of the Toronto-Dominion Bank of Canada, has pointed out in a recent speech that the United States citizens pay less income tax. The Minister has overlooked these sorts of exemptions and deductions: (1) they can deduct their taxes with reference to real estate; (2) they can deduct interest against any mortgage; (3) they can deduct interest against any consumer goods; (4) they can deduct any interest; (5) they can deduct $600 exemption per child instead of $300; (6) they have greater medical exemptions by way of drug, dental and optical expenses. In fact, deductions in the United States are so generous that you just cannot compare our income tax rates with theirs; and when the President of the Toronto-Dominion Bank in this country says in a recent speech that they pay less tax per capita per dollar, then I will take his word for it.
In conclusion, I ask these questions: Can it be against Canada's interest to defeat a Government which deceived the Canadian people over the devaluation of the dollar?
Can it be against Canada's interest to defeat a Government which stated categorically that the imbalance of payments must be brought into balance, and then did nothing about it? [DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Can it be against Canada's interest to defeat a Government which declared war on the poor, instead of war on poverty, and made a mockery out of the United States slogan?
Can it be against Canada's interest to defeat a Government which implemented a sales tax increase in the cost of productivity to the country, and refuses in the face of favourable economic facts to abolish it?
Can it be against Canada's interest to defeat a Government whose main leaders, when in the opposition, spread dissension, gloom and doom, at a time when we had an exchange crisis similar to the one of 1947, in the days of Mr. Abbott, and similar to that crisis which Great Britain is going through at this time? Destroy the country, but elect Liberals; victory at all costs, say the Grits-irrespective of responsibility and irrespective of the results.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought that after the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) the Liberals would have followed more
May 3, 1965	COMMONS
assiduously this debate, which lasts but six days. At present, there are 14 Liberal members, out of a total of 129, present in the house; and some ten minutes ago, there were but five. Only one minister is here in his seat, namely, the Minister of Finance. Among 23 cabinet ministers, only one is here to listen to what the opposition has to say against the budget speech.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Liberals are ashamed of this budget to the extent that they remain in their offices rather than in the chamber to hear-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stupidities.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Listen to the hon. member for Longueuil. Fortunately, he will not be here after next election, and we will no longer hear his nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has no right to make remarks concerning hon. members who are present in the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was not making remarks, Mr. Speaker, but merely mentioning a fact.
I intended to move-but I am precluded from so doing by the standing orders-an amendment to the amendment of the Conservative party, and it would have read as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the phrase "economic problems of the country" and inserting instead the following words: by omitting to present a measure so that requirements of public capitaland not private capital.
I see the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) who is familiar with public capital.
-of public capital be met by the creation of new credits without interest by the Bank of Canada.
I am convinced that the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska understands that point and would have supported such a measure. But I am not allowed by parliamentary procedure to move a subamendment because we are discussing the budget.
As my first comment, after a review of the budget brought forward by the Minister of Finance Monday night, April 26, I should like to say that, in general terms, that budget is a colossal hoax and the information media that made favourable comments on that budget have knowingly misled the Canadian taxpayers. We saw the headlines in some papers:
10 per cent income tax reduction.
DEBATES	847
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
And the C.B.C. comments:
The Liberal government, in its great generosity, gave the Canadian taxpayer a 10 per cent tax reduction.
It was with unconcealed pleasure, in fact, that commentators from those information media, especially those who are handsomely paid by the C.B.C. out of the taxpayers' money, presented as a miraculous measure the 10 per cent cut on personal income tax announced by the Minister of Finance.
Here are a few figures showing that the praise given to the Minister of Finance is totally uncalled for and unjustified. On page 441 of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, appear the following examples of the reduction granted to single taxpayers without dependants:
$2,000 income, $10 reduction; $5,000 income, $59 reduction; $10,000 income, $180 reduction; $20,000 income, $565 reduction.
Consequently, the reduction on an income of $5,000 is six times bigger than that on an income one third as high, $2,000. On an income of $10,000, which is five times the last mentioned amount, the tax relief is 18 times greater and on an income ten times that same amount, the relief is 56.5 times higher.
Such is the anti-social justice or the social injustice of the present Liberal government.
Let us come now to the reduction granted the average taxpayer, the father of two children in receipt of family allowances. Let us take the case of the father of a family who has a budget deficit-I hope the minister understands what I mean here-of a salaried worker who cannot make both ends meet because his income is too low, and let us see how generously he is treated by the Liberal government and by the Minister of Finance whose speech seems to have been dictated by Bay street financiers, in Toronto.
On a $3,000 income, an annual reduction of $3 is given a little less than one cent a day. On the other hand, on a $10,000 income, the reduction is $135; and on $15,000 income, it is $493, that is 164 times more than that granted the poor father of a family earning only $3,000 per year.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, according to table 25, on page 41 of budget papers tabled by the Minister of Finance, the consumer price index increased by 3.7 during the last two years alone. For the low wage earner who is single and earns $2,000 a year, that increase, that price inflation means that he must spend
May 3, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Caouette $74 more a year on those consumer goods and services he requires. Now, the Minister of Finance, in his great generosity, grants him a $10 reduction per year. Under the Liberal regime, the poor are becoming poorer than before-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-because there is absolutely nothing in the budget to increase the purchasing power of people with an income below $3,000. Absolutely nothing to assist those who need it most.
To take the example given by the minister, let us consider the case of a family head with two children eligible for family allowances and earning $3,000 per year-assuming that he is a taxpayer, because of his low income-out of all his earnings, that man must spend on consumer goods and services $111 more, the amount which is taken off his income by the increase in the consumer price index alone. The Minister of Finance specifically stated, in his budget speech of April 26 last, that in his great generosity, he was granting that man a tax reduction of $3 per year, while he has to spend $111 more to maintain the same standard of living as two years ago.
With the Liberals, the poor are becoming poorer, the situation of small wage earners is becoming more precarious, and times will be harder in thousands of Canadian homes.
With the budget which was presented this year, do the millionaires, or those whose income is $35,000, such as the ministers, or members of Parliament, earning $18,000 a year, need personal income tax deductions? Or would it not rather be the small wage earners, the small taxpayers, the poor people who must receive special care from the government, a government which instead of applying social injustice or an antisocial policy, as the one which is being offered to us now, should see to it that the poorer members of our population, the small wage earners, the families with small income, be granted more attention by the Government? Those are the people upon whom the Minister of Finance should pay attention.
But the social injustice and the antisocial and antifamily policy of the government, which claims that it is "liberal", is even more evident when it grants higher tax reductions to those who have no family responsibilities.
Here are a few instances of this so-called "liberal" policy, which I call antisocial and antifamily: for a single person whose annual

salary is $3,000, the tax reduction is $24 a year; for a married man with no dependants, it is $10 a year, and if he has two dependants, it is $3 per year. A single person earning $4,000 a year will save $40; a married person without dependants, $24 per year, and a married person with two dependants, $15 per year. A single person earning $5,000 a year will save $59; a married person without dependants has a reduction of $40, and if he has two dependants, his reduction is $30.
With such an antifamily policy, it will not be necessary for the government to take direct birth control measures, as is done in other countries. This is an indirect measure to attain the same objective.
In the speech from the throne, much is made about the war against poverty, want and destitution, but the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance told us that the speech from the throne did not necessarily refer to poverty-stricken people, but rather to the lack of opportunities, the lack of education, the lack of training, and actually not to the lack of purchasing power among Canadians.
Poverty and destitution are unknown in Canada.
This is what the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance actually told the house, whereas the speech from the throne referred to war against poverty and destitution as they exist. The Liberals no longer know what terms to use, because they are confused and mixed up.
Is it by favouring the rich and disregarding the poor that the government intends to fight poverty and destitution? Is it by making the rich richer and the poor poorer that the government proposes to set up a socially fair economic order, a system enabling everyone to enjoy the wealth resulting from our national production?
Is it by reducing the purchasing power of the poor that the government policies of the Liberal party will fight poverty? Is it by reducing the taxes of rich people that we shall enrich the poor? Is it by giving to the rich that we shall help the poor, those who need to be looked after by the government, a government which claims to be government of the people, when it is controlled by finance and for finance? Is it by granting reductions to the more affluent classes of society that the government means to establish a socially fair economic order?
On many occasions, we have heard the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), the minis-
May 3, 1965

ter of the Liberal new guard, the minister who does not get along with others, the minister who wants to smash the old guard of the Canadian Liberal party, who said recently in the province of Quebec that he would not follow the old guard, the old gang of the Liberal party. Has the Minister of Forestry done anything in the house ever since he became a member of the cabinet?
On the contrary, government policies seem designed only to benefit the mighty and the rich and to crush the poor further. In so doing, the Liberal government is paving the way for an unprecedented social and economic disorder, after allowing disorder and brutality to prevail in the political field and in the relationship between the two founding races of our country.
After initiating policies conducive to confusion and national dissension, the Liberal government is in the course of laying down the basis of unprecedented economic and social disorder by allowing the less favoured groups of our population to be reduced to increasingly abject economic conditions.
In a speech delivered two weeks ago before thousands of pilgrims gathered at St. Peter's in Rome, Pope Paul VI said:
We must have the virtues conducive to peace, the capacity to give precedence to human over economic values
Human values, Mr. Speaker, that means the value of all individuals, of every man, woman and child, not only the wealthy and the powerful; the value of the individual must have precedence over economic values, over financial values, over money.
The concern about all human beings, without an exception, taking advantage of riches within reach and designed for them, must have precedence over the concern to safeguard the tyranny of the dollar sign, the tyranny of the makers of money and of credit. [DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In a joint letter sent on March 22, 1964, that is barely a year ago, to the President of the United States, 22 prominent personalities of the country warned him that if the solutions he advocated were not applied within a short time, which meant as soon as possible, the American nation would be faced with an unprecedented economic and social disaster. And we know that Canada follows in the wake of the United States.
Here are some of the personalities who signed that letter: Mr. Ralph Helstein, of Chicago, president of the United Packing House Workers; Mr. Gunner Myrdal, Swedish
The Budget-Mr. Caouette economist, of the Institute for International Economic Study; Mr. Ben B. Seligman, director of the Department of Education and Research, Retail Clerks International Association; Mr. Robert Theobald, consulting economist, of New York; Mr. Stuart Hugues, professor of history at Harvard University; Mr. Linus Pauling, Nobel Peace prize winner; Mr. John William Ward, professor of history at Princeton University. What did those prominent personalities say? I quote:

As a first step to a new consensus it is essential to recognize that the traditional link between jobs and incomes is being broken.
The economy of abundance can sustain all citizens in comfort and economic security whether or not they engage in what is commonly reckoned as work. Wealth produced by machines rather than by men is still wealth. We urge therefore that society through its appropriate legal and governmental institutions, undertake the unqualified commitment to provide each individual and every family with an adequate income as a matter of right, not a gift.

Mr. Speaker, it must be noted that no longer are full employment and a high employment level being mentioned; but an assured income is being advocated, which is far removed from the present government policies. In fact, what did the Minister of Finance say in his speech:
When this government first came into office we stated a number of economic objectives. Our first goal was a high level of employment for Canadians-
"A high level of employment"; that is the aim of the government as recognized by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech.
On the other hand, we of the Ralliement Creditiste do not believe that the first objective of the government or of the present industrial system is to provide jobs. On the contrary, we believe that the purpose of economic activities is to promote the welfare of the home, of the family, in short, of the consumers.
Mr. Speaker, may I quote from a report submitted to the general meeting of the churches of Scotland in 1962 by a group of theologians, economists and sociologists. Here is an excerpt from this report entitled "Money, a Christian View":
We have come to believe that any job Is better than no job at all and that the main purpose of any economic policy is to create employment. In our opinion, the purpose of production is consumption: and while employment is part of this process, it is not the main factor. From a Christian point of view, man should not have to do a job which a machine could perform.
May 3, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Caouette
Those are the words of economists and sociologists. This is exactly what supporters of what is called Social Credit stand for. We are indeed in good company.
What is the opinion of Rev. Father Georges Henri Levesque, Dominican, a former joint chairman of the Massey-Levesque royal commission? In a pamphlet published by "Les Editions du Levrier" in Ottawa, in 1936, Rev. Father Levesque said this about Social Credit and the policies advocated by its founder, Major C. H. Douglas, and I quote:
But it is not enough for Douglas to set his economics in a spiritual setting or environment and to direct it, as it were, from the outside, toward spiritual values. He incorporates this spiritualistic finality to the very core of his system. This system is entirely based on this great Christian principle: the true purpose of any economic activity is to satisfy human needs and not to create wealth for wealth's sake.
The true aim of production and distribution, as Douglas often says, is consumption. The function of an economic system is to supply adequate goods to the consumers who really need them.
All the reforms advocated by Douglas, adds Father Levesque, spring from the argument regarding the supremacy of the consumers and tend to put the economy at the service of man, of all men.
And in his booklet, Father Levesque added this for the newspapermen and politicians who describe Social Credit in a fantastic and false manner:
Therefore, when newspapermen, well paid by political parties, claim that Social Credit is antiChristian socialism, beware of their theological philosophy. It is usually too rudimentary to give you safe directives. And, in this case, it could not reasonably justify its anathema, especially because it is too interested. When those men become self-appointed theologians, it is in general much less to stand by the revealed truth, than to safeguard the petty interests they defend in their writings. To this end, they will resort to any means.
Beware of them, continued Father Levesque, even when they approach Social Credit from its economic aspect. Reigning politicians see in this movement a growing and threatening political power.
The Minister of Finance is aware of that. I continue:
Bankers see in it the avowed enemy of their valued monopoly. So do not be surprised if their publicists attempt to disprove its doctrine or to ridicule it, which is much easier and requires less intelligence.
Mr. Speaker, in this last part of my speech, I wish to deal briefly with the baneful policy of our present banking system which is the cause of the growing indebtedness of every level of government, corporations and individuals in every class of society. I wish to state that it is precisely on account of the monetary policies of the present government

and the previous ones that Canadians are so heavily taxed and hundreds of thousands of Canadians are destitute and live in abject poverty.
The other day I heard the Minister of Finance speak about our balance of payments with foreign countries, of our international payments. He then blamed the Conservatives as being responsible for the almost intolerable situation existing in Canada.
At this point, I refer to page 45, and more especially to Table 28 of the budget papers tabled by the Minister of Finance.
In looking over this table, we find that in 1956, while the Liberal party was in office in Ottawa, there was a deficit of $1,366 million in our balance of payments. The Liberals were the first to pile up a deficit of a billion dollars in our trade with other countries. And now, they blame others for having exceeded the billion dollar mark after they themselves set such an example.
Mr. Speaker, I want to suggest a few ways of solving this problem by means of the Social Credit policies.
During the fiscal year, according to the estimates of the Minister of Finance, the Liberal government is going "to siphon off" and I use these words advisedly-$6,685 million to say nothing of the non-taxation revenues, which amount to $840 million and the revenues from the old age security tax which amount to $1,145 million.
Such are the amounts of money that the Canadian government is going to take from the pockets of the poor Canadian taxpayer.
And how will those revenues amounting to $8,670 million be chiefly used?
First, for the public debt charges, or the interest paid on the debt: $1,103 million, which is twice the amount that will be earmarked for national health and welfare and almost three times more than the amount that will be spent under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
Mr. Speaker, when we advocated not long ago a full tax exemption to every married person earning less than $5,000 and to all single persons earning less than $2,500, I myself met newspapermen who told me: "It would cost Canada $1.2 or $1.5 billion to grant such exemptions."
But those same newspapermen never asked themselves where Canada got $7 billion during the war to help our allies and try to win the peace which we still have not got. Where did the money required come from then? That does not worry the newspapermen.
May 3, 1965

But the moment one speaks of granting exemptions to the Canadian taxpayers, you hear somebody say:	"But where will the
money come from?"
Debt charges amount to $1,103 million. That is what the government will pay this year to financiers. And let no one try to tell me that the Canadian people will profit by it. Who holds government bonds at present? In a proportion of 90 to 95 per cent, they are deposited in collateral security in Canadian chartered banks. That is where government bonds are, and the government knows it quite well.
Second, our defence expenditures amount to $1,581 million.
Mr. Speaker, when we, Creditistes, ask that family allowances be brought up to the level of the cost of living index since 1945, here is the answer we get: We have no money, we are unable to find the money to increase family allowances. Some people like the hon. Member for Longueuil, the hon. Member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin), the hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Mitchell), and the hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) claim that we cannot afford to raise family allowances. And yet Canada finds it possible to give credit to scores of countries but it cannot do anything for its younger population.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what Liberal members on your right are doing.
With the exception of Creditiste members, no one speaks against the tribute-money that Canadians are forced to pay to bankers; no one protests against the $1,103 million we will have to pay in interest this year.
When it is a question of increasing the national debt by $346 million as in 1961, by $791 million as in 1962, by $691 million as in 1963, by $1,150 million as in 1964 and by approximately $479 million as in 1965, according to the table published in the budget papers which I have here, no one gets alarmed, no one takes exception, no one objects. When it comes to paying interest on bonds, no one stands up to proclaim how nonsensical it is for Canada and the Canadian people to run more and more into debt in a country so rich in natural resources, in goods and services of all kinds. This is an illogical situation, a nonsensical situation of which not only the Creditistes are becoming aware but also high officials of the U.S. administration.
On September 21, 1964, just seven months ago, the banking and credit committee of

The Budget-Mr. Caouette the House of Representatives in the United States introduced a report published by the U.S. government and available in the publication department of the U.S. government. This document, entitled "Money Facts", is made up of 169 questions and answers on the subject of money.
Question No. 69 reads as follows: e (4:40 p.m.)

If the government can issue bonds, why can't it issue money and save the interest?

Here is the answer given by that same committee:

A few clear-headed and firm individuals, such as Abraham Lincoln have insisted that the government should. The late Thomas Edison stated this matter this way "If our nation can issue a dollar bond, it can issue a dollar bill. The element that makes the bond good makes the bill good also."

It is absurd to say that our country can issue $30 million in bonds and not $30 millions in currency. Both are promises to pay: but one promise fattens the usurer and the other helps the people.
However, it has been one of the political facts of life that private banks must be allowed to create the lion's share of the money even if not all the money. Thus there is little opposition to the government's printing bonds and then permitting the banks to create the money with which to buy these bonds: but the proposal that the Government itself create the money instead of the bonds has always set off tremendous political upheavals. For

On example, Lincoln set off a political furore when he insisted upon having the government issue $346 millions in money (the so-called "greenbacks") instead of issuing interest bearing bonds and paying interest on the money.

The following question provides an answer to those who claim that such a solution would cause inflation. It reads as follows:

If the Government issued more money instead of government bonds, isn't there a danger that a government would issue too much money and cause inflation?

This is the answer provided by the U.S. government banking committee:

No. It is no more or no less inflationary for the private banks to create $1 billion of new money than it is for the Government to create $1 billion of new money. Furthermore, as an agency of the Government, the Federal Reserve System decides in any case the total amount of money to be created.

How, they ask, do banks render a service to the government or to the people by buying treasury or government bonds? Here is the answer given by members of the U.S. government committee to this particular question:

No, because they create money, an obligation of government, simply to buy bonds guaranteed by the government. There is no risk involved as there is in loans to businessmen and consumers. Their reward for buying bonds with money they create is the "subsidized" profit they enjoy.

And here is question No. 132, following immediately the above answer:

What is the burden of U.S. government bonds held by the private banking system?
The burden is the heavy bond interest, borne by the taxpayer that goes to the private bankers, when the same amount of money could be created by agency of the government.

Question No. 167 in that same paper, asks which reform is required in the present banking system in the United States. Answers are just in the same vein. We of the Social Credit party have been giving those answers here in Ottawa for a long time. First the reorganization-

The reorganization of the federal reserve board, toward greater responsibility.
May 3, 1965	COMMONS

That is the little gimmick which is going on in Ottawa every Wednesday when controllers of the economic life blood regulate Canada's wealth and purchasing power.

Abolition of the open market.

The actual balance between total credit in circulation and the wealth of Canada.

Co-ordination of monetary with other economic policy.
Financial accountability, via audits. A reappraisal of the "tight money" policies. A lessening of private banks' influence in the Federal Reserve System.

Mr. Speaker, this is exactly what Social Crediters have been demanding for a long time and we will continue to do so until the Minister of Finance and the government understand that it is proper and necessary to help the ordinary citizens who have to live and who are justified in wanting to live in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly to the amendment before the House.
The criticisms that have been made of the budget so far seem to have been directed at single items in the budget proposals, and limited to suggestions that while the objectives set out in the budget speech are desirable the approaches might have been different.
As far as I have been able to detect, however, there has been no comprehensive criticism of basic aims. This is understandable. It would be difficult indeed to criticize in any fundamental way the achievements of the last two years. It would be particularly difficult to criticize Canada's accomplishments in 1964.
The reduction in unemployment in that year was a record of 13.4 per cent, nearly double the rate of reduction accomplished in the United States. The total output of goods and services by Canada last year was 8.9 per cent greater than the year before. This was one third as much again as that achieved by the United States.
The deficit was reduced to $83 million, according to the parliamentary accounts.
DEBATES	853
The Budget-Mr. Gordon There was a surplus of over $300 million, according to the national income accounts. These are the best results for seven years.
I acknowledge the dilemma of hon. gentlemen opposite in attempting to criticize these accomplishments or our plans for ensuring that this phenomenal growth is continued throughout the current year.
Instead, the criticisms-somewhat carping and ungenerous, if I may say so-have been directed at the edges. It is claimed by Opposition spokesmen that despite their sorry record during the six years they were in office, despite the loss of so many of their former leaders-I am thinking of Messrs. Hees and Fulton and Halpenny and Sevigny and Noel Dorion and Fleming, among others-they could do better if only they were to be given a second chance.
I should like to examine three or four of the particular criticisms which have been made. The budget proposes an annual cut of $265 million in personal income taxes. The hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan)-I do not want to be unkind to him in any way but I was going to say, speaking to a brief which sounded at times as if it had been prepared, at least in part, by an association of manufacturers with some slight assistance from a well known Senator,-

The United States taxes shown in this table include the Federal tax and a 5 per cent State tax. I should explain that 37 states plus the District of Columbia impose corporation income taxes at rates ranging from 1 to 10 J per cent. The rate of 5 per cent was chosen because it is imposed by the majority of states-more often that any other rate.
The table shows that corporations with a taxable income of $100,000 or less pay lower taxes in Canada than they do in the United States. At $500,000 of taxable income, the taxes in Canada are $249,850 compared with $246,500 in the United States-a difference of $3,350 or just over 1 per cent. At $1 million

The Budget-Mr. Gordon of taxable income, the Canadian taxes are $509,850 compared with $499,500 in the United States-a difference of $10,350 or 2 per cent.
Capital cost allowances are more generous in Canada than in the United States. Accordingly, I think it safe to say that, on the whole, corporation taxes here are lower than they are across the line. Certainly to suggest they are higher here is incorrect.
I wonder if the Opposition were aware of these facts when they moved the amendment that is before the House?
In arguing that corporation taxes rather than personal income taxes should be cut, I am curious to know whether my hon. friend would have cut the rate for small companies as well as large ones. speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Saint John-Albert) moved:
subtopic: REQUEST FOR YOUTH EXTENSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of underwriting a Youth Extension Program of the Parliament of Canada to (a) promote and nurture an interest among the youth of Canada in the principles of our Constitution, the political liberties which root and support our social, civic and economic liberties, the self-denying duties of selfgovernment, and in the evolutionary role of the Monarchy; (b) promote relief in the power of reason as applied through public discussion as preferable to silence coerced by law-the argument of force in its worst form: and so answer the cry most appealing to youth: "Give us more efficiency; get something done; stop this long-drawn-out parliamentary debate; act; look at Russia-imitate them; let the arbitrary forces prevail over the deliberative." (c) provide annual seminars for young Canadians from shore-to-shore under the supervision of M.P.'s and officers of the House of Commons and Senate to gain insight into, and understanding of, the workings of government in deliberation and action.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is quite lengthy but as it is self-explanatory and will appear in Hansard my remarks will be quite brief. This is an appropriate time to bring it forward because of the recent announcement of the establishment of the Company of Young Canadians.
I speak generally about the problems of youth from my experience as President for a number of years of the youth branch of a wing of our political party, and it is my impression that one of the greatest difficulties which has faced youth in the post-war period has been that they did not have the outlet for their energies that we had in the war years. I hesitate to use the term "juvenile deliquency"; someone has suggested that it might be more appropriate to refer to "parental delinquency". An illustration of this term was recently given in a story about a public opinion poll in which parents were called at their home in the evening and each one questioned to see whether they knew where their children were. The first six calls were answered by children who said they did not know where their parents were, that they were out.
May 3, 1965	COMMONS
There is great urgency to this problem of youth. I feel we have failed to give the subject proper attention. We all know the sort of headlines of late which have appeared in the press. There have been sit-down strikes, demonstrations and revolts. In my opinion the culmination was reached the other day, when in Russia, some of the parents and older people who were attempting to go to Church on Easter Sunday were jeered in the streets by their children. Therefore I would recommend in a general way that full study and research continue into this problem. The report on juvenile deliquency, we are informed, will be available shortly, after a great delay which we all regret. The Vanier Council on the Family is continuing its work. There should also be a greater appreciation of the role of law enforcement. The R.C.M.P. and police officers are in great disrepute because they are the only ones who say no to our young children. There should be greater family participation in sports and in outdoor life. There should be a reassessment by parents of material things and status symbols. We must strive to strengthen our own institutions of honesty, integrity, unselfishness and, above all, respect for authority. Lastly, there should be particular outlets for energies of youth, and this is where my motion comes in.
I am proposing that an annual seminar, as outlined in my motion, be held each year. This would be a combination of the Rotary adventure and citizenship. A model parliament is to be set up in 1967, as proposed by Bill Fair of Saskatchewan, and this could be held when Parliament opens. It is to be patterned on the American Hearst Foundation Seminar and I hope private business will also become interested in it.
I envisage a three to five day seminar. The R.C.M.P. and military could look after our young people who would come here from other parts of Canada. I should like to see the Supreme Court included in the plans. Many Members of Parliament have already shown interest in bringing young people from their ridings to Ottawa. I recall that the former Minister of Finance, Hon. Donald Fleming, did this each year, and I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) sponsors young people from his riding each year. This would supplement the idea which has been put forward by others before me and make it a permanent occasion.
It has three particular advantages. First, it would be a way of dealing with the obvious
DEBATES	855
The Budget-Mr. Ian Watson restlessness of youth. Boredom and social pressure would be put aside and the angry young men could play their part more constructively in our parliamentary process. Second, it would provide greater knowledge of our parliamentary institution which is surely needed. The role of the monarchy, which is misunderstood by our youth today, could be dressed up and presented to our young people in a modern way. Third-and this is very important-it is difficult for people from east and west to obtain the money required to come to Ottawa, and my motion would provide for some sort of fund or subsidy to be set up for this worthwhile cause for each Province from shore to shore. Our generation has the opportunity to improve itself, and I reckon we can either strengthen our values and give our youth some guideposts and memories for their peerless future or we can do nothing at all.
I hope that this idea will commend itself to all Members of this House and will go to repair some of the breakdown in understanding which has taken place between adolescents and older people.
Therefore I propose that the Government underwrite a full Youth Extension Program as outlined in my motion. This will demonstrate that we are concerned with the welfare of youth and would tangibly recognize the importance they hold in our future and in the future of nations such as ours, with I hope the result they will be presented with an enthusiastic challenge for their vigour and energy, and in turn may pass on the best, and not the worst, of our system of Government.
