speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. Member who has just spoken for the suggestion which he has just put before the House. I think all of us in this House have realized for some time, certainly since we have been here, that throughout Canada there is a desire among our youth for opportunity for service, and for opportunity to participate more fully in Canadian life. Youth today feels a little left out of things. There is an abysmal amount of ignorance about our parliamentary institutions, and I am convinced that the hon. Member's suggestion should be seriously considered by the Government. I suggest that the Ministry to take up this suggestion should be the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
During the last two or three months I have been quite interested to learn of the
May 3. 1965

The Budget-Mr. Ian Watson numerous activities which the Department of Citizenship has been carrying out along this line for several years. They have considerable staff working on youth problems and acting in an advisory capacity to youth organizations across the country. I would think that the suggestion the hon. Member has made would fit in with the present activities of the Department of Citizenship, and within the present framework it would be a fairly simple matter to hold the type of seminar he is suggesting by 1967. Those of us who live fairly close to Ottawa have the opportunity of receiving students here quite frequently during the spring months. I always make a point of having the students addressed by two, three or four Members of Parliament, followed by a question period, and I am convinced that these students leave Ottawa with a better appreciation of how Parliament works. I think a complete study along the lines suggested by the hon. Member would produce results in high schools across this country, and would diminish the disrespect which I think youth today holds for our parliamentary institutions.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
We here in this House, and perhaps I should limit this to the few Members who over the past two years have employed tactics of obstruction, are at least partly responsible for the situation referred to by the hon. Member, in respect of which he suggests that we should cease this long drawn out parliamentary debate, come up with something efficient and get something done. We in this House are partly responsible for that situation. I think the greater part of the responsibility in this regard falls on a limited number of Members in this Chamber.
The Government has, in announcing the proposed establishment of a Company of Young Canadians, taken a long step toward providing Canadian youth with opportunities for service, for which they have been asking at least since the end of World War II. During wartime the youth of this country was called upon to serve this country, but since the end of the last war succeeding generations have felt a lack in Canada of opportunities for service in peacetime. A youth corps or Company of Young Canadians, as has been announced by the Government, I am sure will provide an outlet for the energy of these young Canadians and I hope that such a Company of Young Canadians will be directed by a secretariat, a committee or a commission which could, in turn, make 
recommendations to the Government in respect of all areas of youth interest.
There are several important Government-sponsored plans for youth activity. There is, for example, the Centenary Commission, which is doing a wonderful job arranging for a mass interchange of students among the various Provinces in Canada. This is to take place next year and in 1967, and I hope this student interchange will be encouraged and expanded.
The approach which the Government has been talcing, as far as the Company of Young Canadians is concerned, is one which will involve the obtaining of advice from youth organizations in this country. These organizations are being asked to make suggestions regarding the functions of a Company of Young Canadians, which it would be expected to fulfil. I think this is a proper approach. Too often Governments tend to bring in legislation without really consulting the people who are to be involved. In this case the youth of this country is being asked to make suggestions to the Government. By sending in these suggestions at this time they will in effect be taking part in the creation of this Company of Young Canadians. This is surely the right kind of approach to take in respect of something which is new to the Canadian scene.
I am sure the Government has a number of ideas along the lines of this Company of Young Canadians suggestion, which it will probably develop. We are going to be faced with a number of difficulties in launching an internal youth corps program in Canada, because we must restrict ourselves obviously to areas that are within Federal jurisdiction. We will have to be very careful about overlapping, which means that we must start to work with our Eskimo and Indian population on the reservations and in the villages in which these Canadians live.
Rather than setting up an agency whereby white Canadians from the south will go to the Indian and Eskimo villages, I am personally convinced that we should, as far as possible, be careful to use young Indians and Eskimos in this youth corps Company of Young Canadians. I am sure that any other approach than that will meet with great difficulty.
One of the grave problems in respect of encouraging Indians and Eskimos to take part in this kind of program is the distrust on the part of these native Canadians for white men's intentions. We must use as com-
May 3, 1965

pletely as possible the available Indian and Eskimo talent which now exists. Young Indians and Eskimos in Canada during the past 10 or 15 years have been educated. We now have a large number of these native Canadians graduating from high school, or dropping out from high school courses, although reasonably well educated, and returning to their homes, villages and reserves in areas of the north where there are few available employment opportunities. One of the most useful functions that such a company of young Canadians could fulfil would be the channelling of educated and properly trained young Indians and Eskimos into Northern Affairs work. In these areas there are large groups of very competent and well educated young native Canadians without jobs. These trained personnel should be directed to these areas where they could act in the capacity of career advisers, of whom there is a terrific lack in the north. Most youngsters do not have any idea of the sort of job for which they should train themselves. This is one function that is needed immediately in the north. I am convinced that the Company of Young Canadians should take steps to provide personnel of this type, and I would suggest that where it is at all possible these personnel should be Indian or Eskimo.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
With regard to the external program of the Company of Young Canadians, I think we should work initially through the very excellent framework of CUSO, which has been developed over a number of years. The Government has announced its support for CUSO by spending upward of half a million dollars this year, I believe. I think we will find that the program will become so large that CUSO will not really be able to handle it and that eventually we will require for the external program a combination of CUSO and the Company of Young Canadians.
I am convinced that Canada could not spend its money more wisely than by investing it in such a program. The benefits we would reap abroad, as well as the benefits that our youth who participated in the program would reap, would be beyond compare when contrasted with the military aid type of program which our governments have tended to support in the past. These programs have their place, of course, but dollar for dollar I think nothing will produce as many beneficial results for Canada and the people we are trying to help as the Company of Young Canadians.
The Budget-Mr. Thompson
There is another area where I hope the Company of Young Canadians will be beneficial within Canada, and that is in dealing with problems in areas of rural poverty and also in urban slums. This is a field where we are going to have difficulty because of the provincial jurisdiction involved. The need for career counselling in areas of rural poverty and urban slums is just as pressing as among our young Indian population. I think we can be more useful in this area than in any other.
Canada is a country that is relatively undeveloped and I cannot help but feel that the youth of our country are not taking advantage of our fantastic wilderness areas in the same way that the youth of many European countries and even the youth of the United States do with regard to their own wilderness areas. We may be developing along this line but our people do not really enjoy being outdoors. I think there is room for a Government program. I know that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) has been doing something along the lines of encouraging our youth to make greater use of our national parks, but certainly much more can be done by the Government to encourage the enjoyment by our youth of our wilderness areas and our national parks. I should like to congratulate the hon. Member again for his suggestion. I think it is certainly worthy of consideration and I hope that next year the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will take up his idea and put something into effect along the lines suggested.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) on bringing forward this motion. I believe it is a very commendable one and has a most important objective. With regard to the continuing of a strong system of parliamentary government such as we have in Canada, certainly we who are part of the parliamentary system at this time owe it to those who will take our places to make sure that they have not only a wider knowledge but a deeper understanding of the principles that are involved as part of our responsibilities.
I think most Members of the House are aware of the plans of a group of young people headed by a Mr. William Fair of Saskatoon to include as part of our Centennial celebrations a youth parliament that would sit on or about the 1st of July. In this youth parliament there would be representatives from
May 3. 1965

The Budget-Mr. Thompson every Province who would carry on a mock parliament, so to speak, as part of the Centennial celebrations. I think this idea has been endorsed by all parties in the House and certainly it has been given the endorsa-tion of every provincial Government. In fact, I believe that the provincial Premiers are ahead of us in realizing the importance of such a project. I was going over some of the clippings and letters I have on this subject in my file, and came upon the very definite and well stated comments of the Premier of Prince Edward Island. He said:
The stimulating of interest in public affairs on the part of our younger people and an expanded knowledge of national and international problems confronting governments today would seem to be a very commendable objective. The gathering together of youth delegates whose eligibility would involve a course of training and investigation and their presence as observers on the parliamentary level, as well as the broadening of the conference to take in areas outside of Canada, would seem to be quite worth while.
I think this statement goes right to the heart of the suggestion that has been made in this motion and I believe that all of us should support it. I would hope that the motion could be passed this afternoon because it would indicate our own interest and concern in a wider grasp and a better understanding of the parliamentary set-up. The proposal for a Centennial Youth Parliament envisages that it would be held on the 100th anniversary of Confederation, July 1, and that for every Member of Parliament in the House there would be a member in the Youth Parliament. It is also proposed that His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Cornwall, be invited to attend to represent the Crown. I think this is an excellent suggestion and could well provide the opportunity for Prince Charles to take the first step toward accepting his own responsibilities as heir apparent to the British throne.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Another thing that the youth parliament would emphasize would be a Canadian Youth Week as part of the Centennial program. Not only has this suggestion received rather wide support from those who are Members of the Parliament and Legislatures of Canada, but there is also much support elsewhere. In fact, the committee for the Canadian Assembly of Youth Organizations has discussed this matter and made recommendations. On October 29 of last year they submitted a report to the Centennial Commission recommending such a youth program for Centennial year. They have made

other recommendations also which would strengthen this into more of what I believe this motion intends, that would give administrative support and body to the centennial project. It seems to me that this motion is right in line with that suggestion from the Canadian Assembly of Youth Organizations.
Let us look at the motion briefly, Mr. Speaker. I notice that the first particular objective of it is to promote and nurture an interest among the youth of Canada in the principles of our constitution, the political liberties which root and support our social, civic and economic liberties, the self-denying duties of self-government, and in the evolutionary role of the Monarchy. I think that is well stated, and possibly every Member of this House ought to give it support and support now.
In looking at the second objective, I suggest perhaps that the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) may clarify further his suggestion. He says it should promote relief in the power of reason as applied through public discretion as preferable to silence coerced by law-the argument of force in its worst form. I think I understand what the hon. Member is getting at, but I believe he has beclouded his objective a little of getting a permanent youth extension program set up that would have as its objective the educational study and discussion of the beliefs and functions of the democratic system as they relate to Parliaments and Legislatures.
I would agree, however, completely with the third point. It is to provide annual seminars for young Canadians from shore to shore under the supervision of Members of Parliament and officers of the House of Commons and Senate to gain insight into, and understanding of, the workings of Government in deliberation and action. I feel this is a specific area of need that is so important that it should not be confused with the Company of Young Canadians or some other youth organizations which have legitimate and worthwhile programs. We should not cover the particular area as if the objectives of this motion were to be relegated to that generalized picture. Perhaps in so doing we would miss the vital importance that I understand this motion represents.
I have the opportunity to speak to university groups and high school groups very often, and while I am amazed at the lack of information many of these groups have concerning the functioning of our parliamentary system, on the other hand I am encouraged by the
May 3, 1965
fact there is a hard core of young people who are interested in and concerned with what is taking place on the public scene. I feel we should encourage them and help them in making this particular study one of greater relevance to them. I believe that as some of us see the functioning of this House, we are not too happy with it. Many are concerned that we should have permitted the functioning of the House of Commons to drift along in such a way as to further the general impression across the country at this time that Parliament is not the institution it should be. Parliament, in the democratic system we have in Canada, is the heart throb of democracy. As we lose sight of Parliament, in exactly the same way democracy becomes less effective.
Again, I give my support to this motion. I urge everyone in the House to do likewise. Let us pass it, and let us show the young people of Canada we are actually interested in them, that we want them not only to understand but to become part of the parliamentary system and functioning of Government.

The Minister said that there was nothing to the claim that the 11 per cent sales tax had done so much harm in this country. As reported in the Montreal Gazette of April 28 the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. A. A. Cumming, referred to the budget as a "damp squib budget". I have great faith in Mr. Cumming because he is a native Nova Scotian, and Nova Scotians know what they are talking about. With

The Budget-Mr. MacEwan further reference to the budget Mr. Cum-ming went on to say, as reported in the Gazette:
All in all, while not the shocker that his first budget was, Mr. Gordon's third effort, so far as business and industry are concerned, falls short of the glowing advance billing it was given by the professional kite-flyers.
That is certainly the case. The Minister said that the sales tax would do no harm.
I should like to read a short telegram which was received by the hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Stenson) whose riding is a heavily industrialized area. The telegram is from the Fisher Gauge Works, Peterborough, and it poses a question which I believe the Minister should think about. With reference to the sales tax it says:
Does the House realize that for every dollar paid in wages to tool for production in Canada whether for export or not more than 30 cents must be paid In sales tax alone or nearly one dollar in tax for every hour worked? This raises Canadian labour rates for tooling higher than U.S. rates. It is hardly necessary to wait for the Royal Commission report on taxation to correct this absurd situation.
Another matter referred to by the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings which is very important, especially to the Maritime area, was education. When no change was made in this regard various submissions were put forward from the Maritime Provinces. In particular, the President of Acadia University, a well recognized university, had this to say:
The fact that the budget makes no provision for interim financial help for the universities pending the report of the Bladen Commission is bound to cause profound dismay among those responsible for higher education. Our situation is critical and immediate action is imperative.
The Halifax Chronicle-Herald also had an editorial on the subject headed "Why Wait"; in other words, why wait for later in the spring, do it now. The editorial had this to say in part:
Mr. Gordon could have acted, but chose to wait. We hope that the strong representations made to him to reconsider his decision will bear fruit, and that extra aid designed to last until more permanent measures arising from the Bladen report are implemented, will be announced before Parliament's summer recess.
There is another very important matter which I recall the Minister dealt with in his first budget. He took some pains to deal with the large amount of money set aside for shipbuilding subsidies. We know how important these are to the shipbuilding areas of Canada in the Atlantic Provinces and on the West Coast. We also note that this year there has

been a cutback from $32 million to $27 million in this regard and that an interdepartmental committee has been set up by the Government to study whether the shipbuilding subsidies will be continued. They are being continued for fishing trawlers. Let us hope the Government will continue them for other types of shipbuilding in this country.
When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) issued his statement about February 8 he pointed out that because of the large backlog of work in this country the shipbuilding subsidies could be deferred. I am not inclined to agree with the Minister in this regard. He referred to the naval shipbuilding work which will be forthcoming but I do not think we can hope for much from that. I put a question on the Order Paper for the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) inquiring when the first keel would be laid under the new shipbuilding program and the answer I received was that it would be in 1966. After all, there are only four of these destroyer escorts and apparently two transport ships that will be built, and we certainly have more than six shipyards in the country. Therefore I hope that the committee which has been set up will not take too long to report. Otherwise, the amount of work will drop off, and we all know what a terrific amount of employment has been provided by the shipbuilding subsidy program introduced by the former government.
All I need to do is to point to the shipyard in my own area, Ferguson Industries in Pictou. I think they are on their fourth trawler at the present time. These ships have all been built under the subsidy program and without the program they would not have had anything in their yards. They have had very few refit jobs since the present Government took office. The situation is quite different from the formers days. I submit to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance that the report should be made as soon as possible because the shipbuilding program is important not only to the yards themselves but to the producers throughout Canada of the many components which go into these ships.
With regard to the tax cut, perhaps it will be repetitious if I go into the figures that have been presented. The hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings pointed out that a married man with an income of $3,000 a year and two dependants would save $3 a year. It is also true that nephews, nieces, aunts and uncles have been added to the list of
May 3, 1965
dependants. I am reminded of that old song: "Sisters and brothers and cousins by the dozens are proud of Uncle Sam". Perhaps we might paraphrase that and say: "Nephews and nieces and uncles and aunts are proud of Uncle Walter", but I do not know how proud. That is the extent of the exemptions.
In this regard I would refer to another native Nova Scotian who has aspired to great heights and has achieved them. With regard to the tax cuts, Mr. Donald MacDonald, secretary-treasurer of the Canadian Labour Congress, said that the budget was "thin and unimaginative". He went on to say that "the income tax cut will give most benefit to those in the higher tax brackets".
The other day the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Gratftey) asked the Minister a question regarding inflation, and perhaps the hon. Member will go into this subject in a speech. I should like to quote briefly from Mr. John Meyer's column in the Montreal Gazette of April 27 in which he said in part:
What is significant is that the factories and mills, in spite of their continually expanded facilities, are running at capacity. This is where the inflation risk is to be found, in the pressure of that additional buying power upon limited supply, in the renewal of the old cycle of too many dollars chasing too few goods.
He went on to say:
"It's no good arguing that the inflation risk is worth taking. It's never worth taking, as the experience in the mid-fifties ought to have taught." [DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We know that in the last two years the cost of living in this country has gone up and up. Personal income taxes have been cut in this budget, but the suggestion has been made also that corporate taxes should have been cut in order to reduce the possibility of inflation.
I was going to go into things which the Minister said were done as reported on page 428 of Hansard. Among other things, he pointed out the provision of massive assistance to the Provinces in the fields of technical and vocational training. We know that the former Government brought in a provision to pay up to 75 per cent of the cost of construction of vocational schools, together with the furnishings. The Minister referred also to a vigorous expansion in the loan programs of the Farm Credit Corporation. We know who set up the Farm Credit Corporation and got it cracking. It was done by our Minister of Agriculture of that day. The present Government has just followed these policies.
The Budget-Mr. MacEwan
Of course, the pegging of the dollar is something which the Minister would not want mentioned. Then, reference was made to increased amounts and improved terms for credits and insurance to finance a rapid increase in exports. We know what was done in this field by the former Government, especially to assist exports, by the former Minister of Finance when he helped to obtain an order for steel rails from Mexico which provided a great deal of work for the Sydney steel works.
I could go on and on. He mentioned the Atlantic Development Board. This was established by the former Government. He did not refer to the Atlantic Provinces Adjustment Grants. These were set up by the former Government and have not been rescinded. This indicates the present Government is following all these policies which were good ones for the Atlantic Provinces, and indeed for all of Canada.
I do not want to be too tough on the Minister. I would say this in his favour. He suggested that there will be a tax allowance for companies adopting measures in connection with water pollution, which is an important matter in this country in this day. We know that our water resources are very important, one of the most important resources we have. In adopting this policy, the Minister has made a move in the right direction. The Province of Nova Scotia has set up a water authority to look into this matter. I am sure this provision will be of help to some companies. I know that this water authority in the Province is starting to do a lot of good work in that line.
In so far as the Maritimes are concerned the Minister, of course, is still looked upon with a little bit of suspicion as a result of the Gordon report on economics. He pointed out in his first budget that if the tax incentives, that is accelerated depreciation, and the three year tax holiday did not help the Maritimes, then he did not know what would. Some suggestions have been made that these incentives have brought industry into areas such as my constituency as well as into the Cape Breton area. I am not going to debate that tonight, whether those things have been the factors which brought these industries into the area.
In passing, however, I would say that Industrial Estates, a Crown Company established by the Province, has had a lot to do with it. They had a lot to do with bringing

The Budget-Mr. MacEwan Scott Paper Company to my area by providing water lor that company. Other factors were brought forward by Industrial Estates, such as guaranteeing the bonds for Clairtone, and that must have had something to do with the establishment of that company. I am not going to rely on my own opinion, but I should like to refer to a report from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council to the Atlantic Development Board. In referring to these tax incentives, as reported on page 12, they say:
We noted that tax incentives by themselves are not likely to be a very successful inducement for regional development, and should only form a part of a more general program.
Farther along they say this, and I think this will bear repetition:
Our investigation indicates that during the first three years of location in the Atlantic Provinces a new enterprise is not likely to do much more than meet the "break even" point.. therefore, if it is intended to offer a three year exemption from income tax as an encouragement to industrial development, the exemption should be offered at least during six years from the inception of the new enterprise.
This is nothing new. The hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) made that statement when this matter was brought forward first. May I also quote from an editorial in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of April 24, 1965, which is entitled "Mixed View". I quote:
We look with favour and fear on the news from Ottawa that the Cabinet has reached "firm agreement" to pay direct grants of up to 25 per cent of capital cost to industries locating in areas of high unemployment or low average income.
I think this is the pertinent part, Mr. Speaker.
With favour because capital grants would represent a welcome extension of the tax incentive policy of a three year income tax exemption and accelerated write-offs of the capital cost of machinery, equipment and new buildings acquired by new manufacturing and processing enterprises which located in "designated areas" of high unemployment.
With favour because full benefit from the present policy is only possible when a new industry is able to achieve profits immediately. This rarely happens.
I should like also to refer to an editorial from the local paper the New Glasgow Evening News, which points out that these incentives are advantages not actual benefits to industries. I quote:
Under certain circumstances there are advantages -a much better word under the circumstances than "benefits". If the new plant is a money maker from the start, the Federal Government graciously permits the owners to keep the money they make."

As is pointed out here, Mr. Speaker, the industry must make these profits during the first three years. This is the exception rather than the rule.
In the last few minutes I have at my disposal, I am going to refer to a suggestion which was made by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council to the Atlantic Development Board to the effect that there should be a grant of 25 per cent of the capital cost of new industries. I refer the Minister back to his statement about the first budget when he said that if these incentives do not help he did not know what would. I feel that this organization, APEC, has pointed out what will assist our area a great deal.
Before continuing, I should again like to quote from the APEC submission, pages 3 and 4. I quote:
Areas for assistance should not be chosen simply on the basis of surplus labour without regard to the potential of such areas...
Then, they suggest that the whole Atlantic region should be designated for assistance. APEC pointed out six particular locations and then said:
This selection is based on rather preliminary investigation and we stand ready to accept changes in the light of further examination.
In this regard, I am suggesting that they should include the area in my constituency served by the New Glasgow employment office. Then, on page 4 of the report it is stated:
We suggest also that a like capital grant should be available to the provincial authorities in respect to each advance factory constructed by them on the industrial parks located in the growth centres, and in respect to each factory on the parks constructed by private interests. In addition, we suggest a like grant to each firm now located in the region undertaking expansion which is likely to lead, either directly or indirectly, to additional employment, e (8:40 p.m.)
I think this is true and I recall that just last fall I was visiting the heavy steel plants, in my area where the railway cars, axles and so on are made. I talked to one of the chief executives in that plant, who said he believed that existing plants undergoing extension should also receive grants and incentives. The Minister should bear this in mind. Not only must we attempt to bring in new industry, but we must hold on to the industry which we have. This is clearly pointed out in an editorial in the Evening News where it says that APEC should include our area as one to be given these 25 per cent capital cost grants.
In my area we have heavy steel manufacturing and all kinds of secondary industry.

We have a thermal plant which was enlarged, thanks to the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act which was introduced by the former government. We have cheap power and skilled workers and I contend our area should be given the benefit of these additional grants.

We have a little rocky ground in Pictou county, up in the Garloch area, but in the rest of the county we have heavy industry which should receive these additional capital grants.
My time is just about up, but in conclusion may I repeat we are just a little bit leery of the Minister of Finance because of the royal commission which he headed when he said he was going to give us one way tickets out of the Maritimes. I think he has changed his mind since then. This evening he mentioned tax incentives and accelerated depreciation. I hope he will give consideration to these 25 per cent capital grants for new industries and extend them to existing industries in the Atlantic area. We do not want to be too harsh on him or too suspicious of him.

Member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) pointed out, was touring the area by helicopter last week end. We have lost the Fergus contract to another company and we hope the Minister of Finance will do something for our area. I urge him not to drop the shipbuilding subsidies which mean so much to our shipyards. By retaining them he can do much to help our area.

Mr. Speaker, as you will recall, last week we protested against changing the order of speakers. At that time, in all corners of the house, it was understood that the house leaders of the various parties would get together in order to agree upon the list of speakers on the budget speech. That meeting was held, and it barely lasted 25 minutes; the representatives of the third parties were ready to accept a suitable compromise. We were ready to admit, to a certain extent, some of the requests put forth by the Liberal and Conservative parties, but the representative of the Liberal party, the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) promised us that another meeting would be held today in order to reach an agreement on the list of speakers.
But there was no such meeting. There was no understanding and, under the circumstances, I suggest that the Speaker of the house, whose responsibility it is to protect the minorities, should continue doing so on the basis of the precedents established for two years now in this house, namely that following a spokesman for the Liberal and Conservative parties, a representative of the minor parties would take the floor, and so on. Those were the established precedents.
Moreover, I should like to point out that we were ready to discuss with the government house leader. We were ready to make concessions and to accept compromises, but, unfortunately, the proposed meetings to reach an understanding did not take place.
There was, of course, a short meeting which was called just before the house met Friday morning. We agreed on the procedure to be followed Friday afternoon, but on the understanding that we would meet again

Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege concerning an in-
cident which occurred immediately before the vote and which has occurred in the past as shown by the facts.
Before every vote, the Liberal and Conservative party whips usually wait outside the chamber until they can gather all the members of their party. Then they walk in together through the central door and proceed to the table, so as to indicate that the time has come to take the vote.
But we have noticed that when the Liberal and Conservative parties vote the same way then both whips agree to enter the chamber without notifying the whips or the representatives of the third parties.
Here is my question of privilege: members of third parties are at a serious disadvantage because, unlike the two main parties, they cannot decide when all their members are in the house.
A similar situation occurred about a month ago. We were then told by the Liberal whip that, in future, he would wait until he had heard from us before entering the house. Now, I find that this did not take place this evening and that is why I am asking Your Honour to lay down a rule or determine the practice to be followed in such a case. Is the time when a vote is to begin to be determined by the whips of the two main parties? If such be the case, should not the whip of the official opposition also consult the whips of the smaller parties? In my opinion, sir, it would be a good thing if you were to rule on that matter tonight.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am appreciative of the circumstances and the difficulties with which the Minister of Finance has been faced. I think he should be complimented for the excellent job he has been doing, which was so clearly indicated by his budget speech on Monday last and again by his speech today. [DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
It should be pointed out that in spite of considerable increases in social spending and increased tax sharing arrangements with the Provinces, he has managed to bring order and control to our fiscal accounts. This is. in considerable contrast to the record of recent years.
There were two areas of particular interest to me, Mr. Speaker, that dealing with the Canada Development Corporation and that dealing with the publications legislation. These relate directly to the problem of foreign ownership and control and affect the long-term interests of all Canadians. '
[Mr. Langlols.i

For some years now many Canadians have been increasingly concerned about the degree of foreign ownership in our country. Thoughtful Canadians are concerned not for reasons of narrow nationalism or anti-American sentiment, but because we wonder whether our continued political independence is possible if we allow the key sectors of our economy to fall into the hands of non-residents.
I have no quarrel, Mr. Speaker, with those who argue that American investment has been beneficial to our country and has financed the development of our resources or that this has improved our standard of living. These arguments are undeniable and are the positive effects of foreign capital. We must remember too that we are a young country, a large and only semi-developed nation, and that we require and will continue to require a great deal of development capital to build our communities and industries and to develop our natural resources. What we must consider are the other aspects of foreign capital, the long term effects on our ability to manage and decide our own affairs, the kind of capital we are importing, where and how it is being invested and whether any regulation is desirable or even possible.
It is disquieting to me to realize that some of the key sectors of our economy already are under predominantly foreign control, not because these companies have not on the whole acted as good citizens but because the investment has been concentrated and uneven and has occurred in the most vital and dynamic sectors of our economy. Statistics, for instance, revealing that 45 per cent of manufacturing is controlled by non-residents do not begin to tell the whole story when we realize the key industry in manufacturing, the automotive industry, is almost entirely foreign owned and controlled. There are many other examples of this kind of concentration in the most dynamic and fastest growing industries in our economy, but the problem is particularly more acute if we note that the investment by non-residents has also been concentrated in the hands of American citizens rather than being spread among the nationals of many countries. This being so, it is not difficult to visualize circumstances where the policies of these companies may not be in the best interests of Canadians. If the investments were spread more evenly throughout our economy and distributed among nationals of several countries, the danger of one foreign country's policies adversely affecting Canadians would be minimized. I should point out that Canadian
May 3, 1965	COMMONS
interests may even be affected without deliberate intent, but as a consequence of policy changes in another country.
I do not intend to go into all the ramifications of foreign ownership and the advantages a subsidiary firm has over Canadian competitors, what policies they may have that affect our import-export problem, United States taxation policies and so on. Many of these have been outlined by a variety of authors and economists during the past few years, the most notable of which was the report of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects. I should point out, however, that the parent-subsidiary operation has not given us the most efficient structure in our economy. For instance, we have eight or nine basic chemical industries producing petrochemicals in our country when perhaps two or three at the most would have provided sufficient competition in our own economy and would have made us more competitive in the international market.
Whether or not foreign controlled industries have acted as good citizens, Canadians must weigh the consequences of continued investment by non-residents in the most dynamic sectors of the economy. We must consider, not necessarily what has been but what could be if this trend is allowed to continue, whether our political survival would be possible if our communications media, our financial institutions and the most important industries were all foreign controlled. I happen to believe that here in Canada, through our own political institutions and given our human and natural resources, we can build a society which will be the envy of the world, even the envy of our American friends. I believe also that most Canadians would agree with me, and in fact Maclean's magazine of last June 6 reported on a survey which indicated that 74 per cent of Canadians were in favour of restricting United States take-overs.
Therefore we must not repeat the mistakes of the past, and while foreign investment in the post-war period did provide a base for our high rate of expansion in the '50's, we must make some adjustments to finance the high level of expansion which is expected in the late 1960's and the 1970's. This period of great expansion was predicted by the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects and has been confirmed by the first report of the Economic Council of Canada. It is clear that large amounts of investment capital will continue to be re-

The Budget-Mr. Moreau quired in Canada for some years, but our past experience indicates that we must devise new ways to utilize existing pools of capital in our economy, must encourage Canadians to participate more fully in the ownership of our industries and must obtain what foreign capital is required more in debenture form rather than in equity investment.
Our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has already taken steps to restrict the equity ownership of our financial institutions and has, through an adjustment on withholding taxes on dividends, given incentives to subsidiaries of foreign owned companies to make their shares available to Canadian residents. We have also broadened the investment powers of some of our financial institutions such as trust and insurance companies who control very large pools of capital in our country.
We have in the present budget proposals a further important step in the Canada Development Corporation. This Corporation is designed primarily to encourage Canadians to participate in the ownership and development of our fast growing economy. The Minister of Finance has indicated that the Canada Development Corporation would have two essential aims: First, to prevent takeovers of existing Canadian concerns either permanently or temporarily until suitable resident ownership can be found and, second, to provide a pool of investment capital to finance new, large scale developments or at least share in these developments with other investment companies. I would add a third objective, that of the substitution of foreign debt capital for foreign equity capital by debenture borrowing if necessary in foreign money markets. I would hope that in setting up the powers of the corporation this would not be overlooked.
We can all recall some notable examples of the take-over situation and the public outcrys which resulted. Some recent examples were Canadian Oil and Labatt Breweries. In most cases, if not all, there was not a Canadian management group who could assemble the necessary finances in the time available to compete with a well timed and well executed take-over bid by a foreign controlled company.
We can also recall some startling and major developments in our resource industries where insufficient capital was available in Canada to finance these industries into production. There were also other considerations but the major limitation was the lack of capital.

In some cases, Mr. Speaker, the discoveries and initiative were provided by Canadians who had to turn to the United States for development capital. This capital was not provided as loans but came in the form of equity investment and control of the industries involved. It is important to note here that the so-called American know-how was really provided by Canadians in many of these industries.
This, then, is the role which I anticipate this Canada Development Corporation will fulfil and which it is intended to fulfil. We must, therefore, now consider carefully the mechanism which will allow it to succeed in fulfilling its intended role. If it is to succeed in preventing a take-over, it must have the confidence and support of the business community, otherwise the directors would not have the intimate and prior knowledge required to act in time. It is therefore essential that the directors be appointed from among our top financial and business leaders. Also, it would not be desirable to have too great a degree of Government participation and control. There are additional reasons for limiting Government participation, which I shall go into further, but certainly the 10 per cent Government participation outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) should dispel any fears of massive Government intrusion into business, or back-door socialism.
Another consideration is the size of the fund and how best to encourage Canadians from all walks of life to participate. It must have sufficient funds to undertake the largest of new developments or the take-over of the largest size corporations, either on its own or in partnership with one or more existing financial groups. A billion dollars would seem to be adequate capitalization, provided the Corporation is given the power to borrow debenture money. Provision should also be made in the capitalization for bond issues with convertibility provisions or for bonds with common share rights, subject to the

decision of the directors. This could be used also to encourage investment by many of our citizens who like some guaranteed returns, or who by reason of age or circumstances may not feel that the common shares would meet their particular needs. I feel also that while the shares should be available to institutional buyers such as insurance companies, pension trusts and so on, the first offerings should be made to individuals on the broadest base possible. We should, for instance, make provision for purchase by payroll deductions much in the same way that Canada Savings Bonds are offered.
I believe thousands of Canadians will welcome the opportunity to invest in our country, particularly if they feel confident that they are investing in a Corporation which has a solid base and good sponsorship. The decision to sell Polymer to the Canada Development Corporation was a good one, in that it provides a sound base for the Canada Development Corporation and it is in the best interests of Polymer. I am sure that progressive management of that Crown Company will welcome this proposal. They will be able to participate in secondary manufacturing ventures arising out of the petrochemical industry, if desirable, without the criticism that there is Government intrusion into business, and the move will also enable them to play a more aggressive part in setting up subsidiaries internationally.
Although, Mr. Speaker, the Canada Development Corporation should not become a depository for troublesome Crown Corporations, I hope the Government and the directors of the Corporation will look carefully at some other Crown Corporations. The Government should consider whether the best interests of these Crown Companies might not be better served by dissociating them from the Government. The directors would then have to consider whether they were a good investment, and would make the decision as to the advisability of buying.
I suggest that Eldorado is in this position, and with an improved outlook for uranium the longer term outlook of the company and the community involved must be considered. Under Government control, the company is seriously limited in its exploration efforts and in its attempts to obtain production contracts in competition with other producers. Without markets and an aggressive exploration program, the company and the dependant community are doomed.
We should consider also the sale of Air Canada to the Canada Development Corpora-

tion if they could also purchase C.P.A. Canada's best interests would be better served by one air line, and certainly the job of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), of formulating an air policy, would be much simplified.
Whatever the result of these and other proposals, the decision to buy must be left with the directors of the Canada Development Corporation. The Corporation, if it is to succeed in encouraging Canadians to participate in our future, must take an investor's view. We must appoint top management people to the Board of Directors and they must have the freedom to work in close cooperation with existing investment companies and financial institutions. We should encourage also the Canada Development Corporation to even participate with foreign owned companies who may have taken the initiative in a development project.
The Canada Development Corporation could also take on the role of placing, over a period of time with Canadian buyers, shares of a foreign controlled company who desired to qualify under the 25 per cent Canadian ownership provisions. Many business leaders have felt that stock issues from some of these subsidiaries would be too large to place in Canada, although the experience of Union Carbide would seem to dispel these fears.
The Canada Development Corporation could also play an important role in establishing those cornerstone industries which provide a base for many secondary manufacturers, such as was done with Polymer when it was first organized. This could be done in co-operation with several smaller competing companies who could collaborate in setting up the basic industry. In many cases a catalyst or focal organization is needed to bring them together, and who may further provide an outside and disinterested balancing force. They could also, through the co-operative enterprise, support basic research on a scale not possible individually and in a way which might allow them to compete more effectively with United States concerns.
These then, Mr. Speaker, are some of the aims and objectives which the Canada Development Corporation would have. I hope that the broadest powers are given to this Corporation so that these and other even more imaginative roles might be fulfilled. Mr. Speaker, on the orders for the day this afternoon I directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) based on the protest made last week by Mr. Claude Edwards, President of the Civil Service Federation of Canada, with respect to the decision of the Government to take no action in the matter of increasing the pensions of civil servants already retired. I regret that the answer given by the Prime Minister this afternoon was one of the two answers which the Liberals have given to this question over the years. Those two answers are as follows: Either the Government says it will consider the matter, or it says it has considered the matter and cannot do anything about it. Today we get the second answer. Many of us do not think this is good enough, and I join in the protest registered by Mr. Edwards which he has made not only on behalf of the Civil Service Federation of Canada but particularly on behalf of our superannuated civil servants.

I draw attention to the words of Mr. Edwards in his recent letter to the Prime Minister, when he said:
In other words, unlike the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States, which have legislated to provide for regular adjustments of civil service pensions to compensate for cost of living increases, your government apparently cannot see that it has a similar responsibility in its role as an employer.
It seems to us, however, that the Government becomes acutely aware of its role as an employer when it comes time to discuss salary revisions for its employees.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a case that surely should not have to be argued in the House of Commons, because some of us have been arguing it for two decades or more. But the need is still there. Justice still calls for these faithful servants of the Federal Government to be recognized as having made their con-

tribution, and to be recognized as deserving of an opportunity to bridge the gap between their pensions and rising costs after they retire.
I realize that in the last 12 months or so there have been two full rounds of considering this matter and reviewing it, but in view of the heightening of the problem, in view of the increasing number of people who believe these pensioners are justified in what they are seeking, and in view of the fact that the Government itself has broken the dam so far as pensions are concerned by declaring that pensions, once put in pay, should be adjusted as the cost of living goes up, I ask the Government will it not now reconsider its position and give to its own retired employees the benefit of the justice they really deserve?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the three minutes available to me I would like to summarize the arguments, some of which were given this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and others which I have organized myself.
The great majority of the 5,000 retired civil servants and of the 5,000 widows of retired civil servants to whom the hon. Member referred are receiving, in addition to pensions as retired civil servants, old age security pensions of $75 a month. This benefit they receive in the same manner as other Canadians over age 70.
Since this Government came to power Parliament has increased the old age security benefit by $10 a month, and this has benefited the majority of these retired civil servants.
Provision has also been made to reduce progressively the age of eligibility for old age security, beginning January 1 next. This will affect beneficially those retired civil servants who have retired on small pensions and have not yet reached the age of 70.
I would also like to refer to the fact that both the Canada Pension Plan benefits and old age security payments will now and for the future be tied to the cost of living index, and therefore the matter of inflation will be looked after.
I should also like to throw some light on the reasons for the large number of small pensions to which the hon. Member referred. These smaller amounts arise from the fact that the employees concerned have worked a relatively short period of time. Pension benefits, as is well known, vary with length
May 3. 1965

of service, and where the period of Government service has been relatively short it is hardly to be expected that the pension benefits will be comparable to those which longer term employees might properly expect to receive.
I repeat again what the Prime Minister stated this afternoon on the question of pension adjustments in relation to increased living costs and reduced purchasing power. The Government wishes to do everything it possibly can to improve the lot of all retired civil servants. However, it has an equal responsibility to all Canadians, and it does not believe that it should discriminate in this matter in favour of its retired civil servants over other retired persons in similar circumstances. In effect, the hon. Member's argument is that retired civil servants should be treated differently from the rest of the population.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-DIRECT PURCHASE OF AUTOMOBILES FOR MOUNTED POLICE
INDUSTRY-DIRECT PURCHASE OF AUTOMOBILES FOR MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
The
subject I wish to discuss in the brief time at my disposal was placed on the agenda in a slightly different form on a previous occasion. I refer to what was said by my hon. friend from Wellington South (Mr. Hales) who drew attention to some pertinent points last Thursday evening, I believe it was. At that time the Minister of Industry was not in the House, and for this reason the discussion came to a somewhat unsatisfactory conclusion. However, the Minister is with us tonight and I hope we may be able to come to grips with this issue and deal with some of the problems arising from the new Government policy on the central purchasing of automobiles, other than military vehicles.
The point which concerns me at the moment is the recent purchase of 127 vehicles from the Ford Motor Company. This contract was originally won by the Chrysler Corporation, but because a strike was taking place in its plant at the time, it was offered to the Ford Motor Company. The price, as I understand it, was a remarkably low price per unit. I am particularly concerned with the unit cost price and perhaps the Minister can provide us with information on this subject when he replies.
There is another aspect of this central purchasing procedure which seems to have been overlooked by the Government. It is this. It automatically puts the Government of Canada, through Crown Assets Corporation, into
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the used car merchandising business. Already I have received from my Province complaints that the R.C.M.P., for whom the vehicles were purchased, are offering used automobiles for sale. Other Members of Parliament from Manitoba have received similar complaints. This situation presents many difficulties. First of all it leads to the breaking of the agreement undertaken by every dealer franchised by the manufacturer concerned. Even worse, from the standpoint of dealers operating in the Province of Manitoba, it breaks the law of the Province concerning the merchandising of used cars.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
Section 12 of the Manitoba Highway Traffic Act says:
No person shall carry on business as dealer or wrecker unless he is the permittee named in a valid and subsisting permit for the purpose issued to him by the registrar, and has paid the fee therefor prescribed in Schedule A.
I want to make it clear that I am not against central purchasing. Indeed, I think that the plan which was initiated about three or four years ago is the ideal approach to this problem. It makes it possible for the Government to have central purchasing to the extent that the manufacturing companies concerned-and this only involved the Big Three-were able to process the tenders, and each one of the three in turn submitted the lowest tender on the purchase of vehicles to the Government. It was done on this basis because it was appreciated that an important part of the sale of an automobile is the warranty, and the servicing which goes on after the sale has been completed. With the expanded warranties and with the improved guarantees this is all the more important at the present time.
So we have this further difficulty. The Government, it would seem, is now purchasing direct from the manufacturers. The franchised dealers are being bypassed, in contravention of the agreement they have with their manufacturers. In my Province at least it places the Government of Canada in the used car business, which is contrary to the Manitoba Highway Traffic Act.

Yes, without a licence. I do not see how the Government of Canada could be issued a licence, either, because the same section of the Act says that the registrar can use his discretion in determining the issuance thereof.

speechtext: How do you dispose of the used car?

maintopic: INDUSTRY-DIRECT PURCHASE OF AUTOMOBILES FOR MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
The dealer does.
There is one other aspect of the matter, and I want to give the Minister sufficient time to reply. The Ford Motor Company, the Company concerned in this particular sale of 127 cars to the H.C.M.P., is in the process of transferring all its purchasing operation to the Detroit factory. That means that the Government will be dealing direct with a United States company. For the life of me I cannot see how this is being fair to the company itself. I am sure that Ford of Canada is anxious to live up to the obligations which it assumes in this very precise statement in the dealer agreement, a copy of which I have in my hand; but obviously they are being forced, because of pressure from the Government. This was obvious in this case, where Chrysler originally had the deal and it was turned over to Ford because of the strike in the Chrysler plant. I trust that the Government will return to the plan which I believe was operating successfully before.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: INDUSTRY-DIRECT PURCHASE OF AUTOMOBILES FOR MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just let me correct what appears to be one small error. A purchase of 127 cars has not been made for the R.C.M.P. Tenders have been called but no contract has been awarded. There have been two earlier tenders called and two earlier contracts awarded. Neither of them was for the number quoted by the hon. gentleman, 127.
The hon. Member has asked what were the unit prices in respect of the 127 vehicles. I can give him the top and bottom prices for the earlier contracts, but not for the 127, as no contract has yet been awarded. In the case of the earlier contracts, which were for the R.C.M.P., for the first 158 vehicles, including 151 sedans and seven station wagons, the prices ranged from $2,209.40 for a two-door sedan delivered at Toronto to $2,865.40 for a four-door station wagon delivered in Nelson, British Columbia.
In a subsequent tender for 171 vehicles, including 155 sedans, nine station wagons and seven half-ton trucks, the range of prices was from $2,172 for a two-door sedan delivered in Toronto to $2,799 for a four-door station wagon delivered in Nelson. In addition there was a half-ton truck, four by four, priced at $3,326. I think that will give an indication of prices.
The new policy has been entered into as a consequence of a recommendation made by

the Glassco Commission, that the Government should employ, in its acquisition of motorcars for civil departments the techniques and procedures which have been followed, with great success and at considerable savings to the taxpayer, by the Government for a number of years in respect of the purchase of vehicles for the Department of National Defence.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-DIRECT PURCHASE OF AUTOMOBILES FOR MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: Automobile dealers are also taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: INDUSTRY-DIRECT PURCHASE OF AUTOMOBILES FOR MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
The policy followed in respect of the Department of National Defence has been to call for tenders from motor-car manufacturers direct, we propose to invite them to quote prices giving the places of delivery, including in every case manufacturers' warranties, and including in some cases where the Department of National Defence or other Departments have facilities for light repair and overhaul the normal repair warranty, and where the Department of National Defence has no facility of its own for overhaul or repair, to include dealers' warranties, normally or ordinarily known, as I understand it, by the term "policy"-which means that the dealer undertakes to put and keep a car in good running order, during the initial period, at the expense of the dealer and at no expense to the user. The dealer is reimbursed for this by the manufacturer. So that tenders will be called for deliveries to different locations and involve one of three levels of warranty-a warranty to be carried out by the dealer, who is reimbursed for his expenses in this connection by the manufacturer. These expenses are included in the tender price.
In respect of repairs, at the same time the manufacturer will quote a schedule of repair charges authorized for the dealer making the repairs. These repairs are made on an as-needed basis, according to the schedule of prices. The dealer invoices the manufacturer and the manufacturer in turn invoices the Department concerned. This is a scheme which the hon. Member will see does not eliminate the dealers from the chain of operation.
